title: Ninety Minutes of Weights Per Week Cut Dementia Deaths by 27 Per Cent. South Asians Cannot Afford to Ignore This.
excerpt: A 30-year Harvard study of 147,000 adults found that moderate resistance training slashed death from neurological disease, heart disease, and all causes — with a ceiling effect that makes the prescription achievable for anyone.
body:
The largest and longest study ever conducted on strength training and mortality has delivered a message that is simple, specific, and hard to dismiss: ninety minutes of resistance exercise per week is enough to meaningfully extend your life.

Researchers at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health analysed data from 147,374 adults tracked over up to 30 years. They repeatedly measured participants' exercise habits across the follow-up period, giving them a clearer picture of long-term behaviour than most prior studies. The findings, published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine, quantify something the fitness world has long suspected but never proven at this scale.

## The Numbers

Adults who performed between 90 and 119 minutes of resistance training per week had a 13 per cent lower risk of death from any cause compared with those who did none. When the researchers broke down the data by cause, the benefits became more dramatic: a 19 per cent reduction in cardiovascular death and a 27 per cent reduction in death from neurological diseases, the overwhelming majority of which were dementia-related.

The strongest finding came from combining exercise types. Adults who regularly performed both resistance training and aerobic exercise had up to a 45 per cent lower risk of death than those who did little aerobic activity and no strength training at all.

Perhaps just as important: more was not necessarily better. The study found no additional mortality reduction beyond about 120 minutes of resistance training per week. The dose-response curve flattened — meaning the benefit is captured in a modest, achievable window of effort. Two hours of weights a week, three or four sessions, is the practical ceiling.

## Why South Asians Should Pay Special Attention

The data arrives at a moment of particular urgency for South Asian communities, both in the subcontinent and across the diaspora.

South Asians have among the lowest physical activity rates of any global demographic. Studies consistently show that fewer than 15 per cent of South Asian adults in the UK, US, and Canada meet recommended exercise guidelines. The reasons are complex — cultural norms that de-emphasise leisure physical activity, long work hours in sedentary professions (particularly in the technology sector), and a historical absence of strength training from mainstream South Asian fitness culture, which has traditionally favoured walking and yoga.

At the same time, South Asians face disproportionately elevated cardiovascular risk. Heart disease develops a decade earlier in South Asians than in white Europeans, driven by a combination of genetic predisposition, higher rates of visceral fat at lower body weights, insulin resistance, and dietary factors. The Harvard study's finding that moderate resistance training cut cardiovascular death by 19 per cent hits this population with particular force.

The dementia angle is equally compelling. India is home to an estimated 8.8 million people living with dementia, a number projected to nearly triple by 2050. Among NRIs in the West, dementia is emerging as the defining health challenge of ageing — and one for which pharmacological options remain limited. A 27 per cent reduction in neurological death from an intervention that requires no medication, no clinic visit, and no special equipment is a public health finding that deserves to penetrate every gurdwara, temple community centre, and diaspora WhatsApp group.

## What Counts as Resistance Training

The study defined resistance training broadly. It includes lifting weights (barbells, dumbbells, machines), using resistance bands, bodyweight exercises like push-ups and squats, and even heavy household and garden work. You do not need a gym membership to hit 90 minutes a week.

"The conversation about longevity often focuses on living longer, but I believe the more important goal is maintaining the strength, mobility, independence, and vitality to fully participate in life as we age," said Josephine Hunt, founder of The Resilience Revolution and a fitness expert not involved in the study.

## The Prescription

The practical takeaway is precise: aim for 90 to 120 minutes of resistance training per week, spread across three or four sessions, and combine it with regular aerobic exercise — walking, cycling, swimming, whatever you will actually do. The study suggests diminishing returns beyond 120 minutes, so this is not a call for extreme gym culture. It is a call for consistency.

For a community that faces elevated cardiovascular risk, rising dementia prevalence, and deeply entrenched sedentary habits, the evidence is now difficult to set aside.

*Sources: British Journal of Sports Medicine, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Fox News Digital*
